result: The study established eccentricity-dependent discrimination thresholds during fixation, with tilt angles increasing from 4.42±0.86° at fixation to 14.10±1.40° at ~15.3-16.2 dva eccentricity.
evaluation: Claims C30 and C31 report threshold measurements from a preliminary task designed to equate task difficulty across eccentricities. The data are clearly presented with means and SEMs, and Figure 1C provides visual confirmation. This methodological calibration is essential for interpreting the main attention mapping results.

result: Presentation of discrimination targets during saccade preparation did not substantially disrupt saccade execution, though saccade latency increased when visual streams overlapped with fixation/saccade targets due to reduced target visibility.
evaluation: Claims C32-C33 report a significant latency difference (p<0.0001) attributed to target visibility, while C36 concludes no disruption of saccade preparation based on latency and accuracy analyses. The interpretation in C33 is reasonable given the overlap manipulation. Statistical tests support the conclusion that discrimination targets did not capture attention away from the saccade task.

result: In the no-cue condition, attention was spatially specific to the saccade target (d'=0.88±0.05 vs 0.42±0.04 average, p<0.0001) without spreading to surrounding positions or to fixation.
evaluation: Claims C37-C40 present converging evidence from the no-cue baseline condition with appropriate statistical comparisons. The spatial specificity test (C39) comparing saccade target to surrounds (p<0.0001) and the null effect at fixation (C40, p=0.8952) are well-documented. Figure 2A-C provides visual confirmation of these patterns.

result: When the cue appeared ~97 ms before saccade (short-cue condition), attention was allocated to the cue and saccade target, but NOT to the remapped location of the cue (d'=0.46±0.07 vs 0.44±0.03, p=0.6886).
evaluation: Claims C41-C44 report the critical short-cue timing condition showing no pre-saccadic remapping. Statistical tests appropriately compare remapped location sensitivity to baseline (p=0.6886, non-significant). The spatial specificity analysis (C42) confirms attention was localized to cue and saccade target but not their surrounds or the remapped location. This is a key negative result supporting the temporal dynamics hypothesis.

result: When the cue appeared ~241 ms before saccade (long-cue condition), attention was allocated to the saccade target, cue, AND the remapped location (d'=0.56±0.07 vs 0.45±0.08, p=0.0072), with all effects being spatially specific.
evaluation: Claims C45-C48 present the main positive remapping finding with appropriate statistics. The critical comparison (C48) shows remapped location sensitivity differs significantly from no-cue baseline (p<0.0038) but not from short-cue condition (p=0.2816), confirming timing-dependence. Spatial specificity tests (C46) support localized attention at all three locations. Figure 2G-I provides visual confirmation.

result: Pre-saccadic remapping requires sufficient processing time (~175+ ms before saccade) and relies on the spatial and temporal dynamics of attention.
evaluation: Claims C8, C9, C49, C62, and C63 synthesize the timing-dependent remapping effects into a coherent conclusion. The data from short vs. long cue conditions (C47-C48) directly support the temporal requirement. The interpretation that remapping depends on attention dynamics (C9, C63) is reasonable given the ~100 ms minimum for attention shifts (C98) and the observed ~175 ms threshold (C97).

result: In the foveal remapping task with adjusted thresholds, attention was deployed to both the saccade target (d'=0.68±0.11, p<0.0001) and the fixation target (d'=0.96±0.02, p<0.0001), with both effects being spatially specific.
evaluation: Claims C52 and C55-C57 report the foveal remapping experiment results. The threshold adjustment (C52: 15.03±2.34° vs 4.42±0.86° in fixation task) addresses the methodological concern about attention withdrawal during saccade preparation. The significant effects at both locations with spatial specificity (C57) support foveal remapping. Figure 4 provides visual confirmation.

result: Three spatially distinct foci of attention were observed (saccade target, cue, remapped location), contradicting the convergent remapping hypothesis of spatially unspecific attention spread around the saccade target.
evaluation: Claims C58-C61 and C64-C65 synthesize the spatial pattern of results. The observation of three separate foci (C64) with spatial specificity (C39, C42, C46) directly contradicts predictions from convergent remapping (C22: 10° spread). The conclusion (C65) is well-supported by the data showing no spread to surrounding positions and attention deployment opposite to the saccade direction.

result: The study achieved high spatial resolution (~4.2 dva spacing) and observed attention deployment opposite to the saccade direction, addressing previous methodological limitations and supporting forward remapping.
evaluation: Claims C24, C81-C83 address the methodological advance over previous behavioral studies. The spatial resolution (C24) is documented, and the observation of attention in the direction opposite to the saccade (C82, C126) is a strong prediction of forward remapping that convergent remapping cannot explain. However, the claim that this 'eliminates' criticism (C81) may be overstated—it improves resolution but doesn't fully resolve all debates.

result: Remapping was observed only when cues appeared >175 ms before saccade, consistent with the ~100 ms minimum time course for attention deployment reported in the literature.
evaluation: Claims C96-C99 link the empirical timing threshold (C97: >175 ms) to established attention dynamics (C98: minimum 100 ms from multiple citations). The reasoning is sound: if attention requires ~100 ms to deploy and remapping is an attentional process, then cues presented <100 ms before saccade would not be remapped pre-saccadically. The data support this prediction.

result: The current results are consistent with early visual area remapping studies (Kusunoki & Goldberg 2003; Nakamura & Colby 2002) but not with LIP studies (Wang et al. 2016), suggesting remapping of attention reflects early visual areas rather than priority maps.
evaluation: Claims C102 and C105-C106 compare current findings to neurophysiology literature. While the absence of intermediate position benefits (C105) contrasts with Wang et al. 2016 (C104), the interpretation that this reflects early visual areas vs. priority maps (C106) is speculative. The authors acknowledge (C66-C67) that behavioral data cannot directly identify neural substrates. This interpretation requires additional evidence.

result: Short probe-saccade intervals in neurophysiology studies may be insufficient for pre-saccadic remapping, with remapping potentially occurring during or after saccades for late-presented stimuli.
evaluation: Claims C108-C112 propose that timing differences explain discrepancies in neurophysiology literature. While the behavioral data (C96-C97) support timing-dependence, the extrapolation to explain neurophysiology results (C108) and the speculation about post-saccadic remapping (C109) go beyond the current data. Citations to Neupane et al. and Yao et al. (C110-C111) provide some support, but this remains largely speculative.

result: Neurophysiology studies should account for attention capture by visual probes and the temporal dynamics of attention when interpreting pre-saccadic receptive field changes.
evaluation: Claims C91-C95 make methodological recommendations based on the current findings and cited literature. The argument that localized probes likely capture attention (C91, citing Theeuwes 1991) and that RFs shift toward attended locations (C92, citing Niebergall et al. 2011; Womelsdorf et al. 2006) is well-supported. The recommendation to consider attention (C93-C94) and temporal dynamics (C95) is reasonable given the demonstrated timing-dependence.

result: High perceptual performance at fixation during saccade preparation, though initially surprising, is consistent with forward remapping of the saccade target to fixation-centered receptive fields.
evaluation: Claims C115-C118 address the foveal remapping finding. The observation (C115) is supported by data (C56) and consistent with previous studies (C116: Knapen et al. 2016; Rolfs et al. 2011). The explanation via forward remapping (C118) is logical: if fixation-centered RFs will process the saccade target post-saccadically, pre-saccadic attention there makes functional sense. However, the alternative threshold explanation (C51-C52) was necessary to reveal this effect.

result: Convergent remapping may not produce broad attention spread but rather spatially specific enhancement at the saccade target through increased neural sampling, potentially reconciling convergent remapping with the current findings.
evaluation: Claims C85-C88 attempt to reconcile convergent remapping with the current data by reinterpreting its behavioral consequences. The citation to computational modeling (C85: Kay et al. 2015) showing that oversampling reduces spatial uncertainty is relevant, but the leap to reinterpreting convergent remapping (C86-C88) is speculative. This reconciliation is proposed but not tested.

result: Future models of space constancy and remapping should incorporate spatial and temporal dynamics of attention.
evaluation: Claims C89, C90, and C122 make recommendations for future work based on the demonstrated importance of attention dynamics. The current findings clearly show timing-dependence (C47-C48, C96-C97) and spatial specificity (C39, C42, C46), supporting the recommendation. The hypothesis (C90) that convergent remapping reflects attention properties is reasonable but requires further testing.

result: The link between behavioral remapping effects and neurophysiology is theoretical; combined behavioral and neuronal recordings are needed to identify neural substrates.
evaluation: Claims C66-C69 appropriately acknowledge the limitations of behavioral studies in identifying neural mechanisms. This is a standard and accurate limitation statement. The recommendation for combined recordings (C69) is reasonable. The claim that findings are relevant to behavioral predictions from neurophysiology (C68) is fair given the detailed spatial mapping.

result: Using an eccentricity-adjusted discrimination task, the study mapped pre-saccadic attention with high spatial resolution, revealing spatially specific attention at fixation, saccade target, cue, and remapped location, with the remapped benefit being smaller but functionally significant.
evaluation: Claims C123-C128 summarize the main methodological approach and findings. The novelty claim (C123) regarding spatial resolution is supported. The summary of findings (C124-C126) accurately reflects the data. The observation about smaller remapped benefit (C127) is evident in the data (C45: 0.56±0.07 at remap vs 0.71±0.06 at cue), and the functional interpretation (C128) is reasonable.

result: The study included 18 participants across two tasks with appropriate sample sizes (25-32 trials per condition per participant) and ethical procedures, with 82-87% of trials included in final analyses.
evaluation: Claims C129-C135 describe participant characteristics, sample sizes, and data inclusion rates. These are straightforward methodological details that appear adequate for the experimental design. The trial numbers (C133: 25.38±0.76 and 16.13±0.42 trials per position) and inclusion rates (C134-C135: 82-87%) are reasonable for psychophysical studies, though more trials per condition would strengthen statistical power.
